info.name: Blog Management API
info.description:
REST API for a blog application with three access levels — Guest, User and Admin.

### Before running

1. Start the API: `npm run dev` (defaults to `http://localhost:5000`).
2. Register an account with the email `admin@example.com` and password `password123`, then promote it in MySQL:

   ```sql
   UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';
   ```
3. Set the `Base_Url` collection variable if your server is not on port 5000.

### Running

Run the whole collection in order. Folder 1 captures every token and id that folders 2–5 depend on, so individual requests will answer 401 if run on their own.

The suite is re-runnable: emails are generated fresh each run, user B is reactivated after being deactivated, and the destructive blog cases create their own throwaway rows.

### What is asserted

Every request checks the status code, the exact response message, and at least one field of the returned data. Negative cases cover 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409. A collection-level script adds a JSON content-type check, a password-leak check and a response-time check to every request, so they can never be forgotten on a new one.

item.name: 5. Cross-cutting
item.description: Behaviour that is not tied to a single endpoint.

item.name: 5.1 An unknown route returns 404

exec: pm.test("message is the expected one", function () {

request.description: Falls through every mounted router to the catch-all handler.

item.name: 5.2 A malformed JSON body returns 400

exec: pm.test("C.2 malformed JSON is a client error, not a server error", function () {
pm.test("C.2b the message names the real problem", function () {

request.description:
The raw body is deliberately invalid JSON. express.json() rejects it before any route runs, so it reaches the global error handler rather than a controller.

Bad input is a client fault, so the handler checks for `entity.parse.failed` and answers 400 instead of blaming the server with a 500.
